prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, trapping neutral atoms at the magic wavelength to measure time at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep the configuration I stated in round 1: a single prize part for B013, the optical lattice clock, to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. What I have changed is the argument and the wording of the citation, not the configuration. The achievement passes the test I apply to every candidate. It is an invention, namely trapping many neutral atoms at the magic wavelength so that the lattice light shift cancels in the clock transition while motional effects are suppressed in the Lamb-Dicke regime. It has been experimentally verified, and the verification is unusually strong because several independent laboratories (RIKEN and Tokyo, JILA, SYRTE, PTB, NIST) build their own clocks and compare them at the 10^-18 level, so the result does not rest on one apparatus. It opens a door in the sense I used in 2023: comparing clocks at this level resolves the gravitational redshift across millimetres, bounds drifts of constants and supports dark-matter searches. The chair's questions mostly concern precedent, and I think the precedent argument is weaker than it first looks. The 2005 prize honoured laser-based precision spectroscopy and the frequency comb, and the 2012 prize honoured control of single quantum systems, including ion clocks. Neither named the use of a magic-wavelength lattice to interrogate a large ensemble of neutral atoms free of Stark and motional shifts, which is a different mechanism and a different experimental regime, and which is what gives the large gain in stability. If the citation is worded around that mechanism it does not repeat an earlier prize. On the attribution question put to us, I read the record as two separable contributions that belong to one achievement: Katori's proposal and first strontium lattice clock, and Ye's demonstration of the accuracy and stability that made the concept a new measurement regime. I cannot verify early priority dates for Lemonde, Takamoto and others from the material before me, so I will not claim more than I can support. On the question of timing, I do not think the redefinition of the second should decide whether to award now. The prize is for the discovery or invention, and the invention has been verified for well over a decade; the redefinition is a use of it, not a condition for it.
statement.case_against: The reservation I take most seriously is my own criterion, that the prize should go to the original work and not to a later group that did it much better. If the committee decides that the decisive contribution is Ye's record performance, built on the comb technology of the 2005 prize, then the credit is closer to refinement than to origination and I would no longer support this pairing. Ye having shared the 2005 prize is not disqualifying in itself, but it makes the wording of the citation matter, because it must name the lattice scheme and its realization and not accuracy records alone. The omission of Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Oates, Derevianko and others is real; a two-name prize is clean but leaves out people who did substantial work, and I cannot say that no priority question remains. Finally, there is the objection from Eriksson and Danielsson that this is a technique and a useful one, rather than a new state of matter or a change in how we picture nature. I accept that it is a lesser kind of discovery than that, but I do not think this should count against an invention that has been verified and that supports tests of fundamental physics.

responses.point: Mehlig asks whether I see the aberration corrector (B015) as a conceptual breakthrough or as a transformative but incremental tool, noting that the 1986 Ruska prize already honoured electron microscopy and that the magic-wavelength principle is more general.
responses.response: That is a fair challenge and I answer it plainly. I regard the corrector as a real invention, since it overturned a limit that had stood since Scherzer, but I accept that the insight is engineering design of a multipole corrector and is not a principle that carries into other areas of physics, as the magic-wavelength condition does. I also accept that the Ruska prize honoured the instrument itself. I am an interested party on B015, so I do not think my first-place ranking should carry weight, and I would not press for it against the weight of the committee. I keep it as an alternative, not as part of my configuration.

responses.point: Pearce notes that the most broadly supported candidate is not necessarily the most important one, that support may reflect clear attribution as much as scientific weight, and that the Higgs discovery (B001) arguably has greater weight but a structurally hard attribution problem.
responses.response: I agree that support counts should not stand in for scientific judgment, and I have tried to base my position on the merits of the achievement and not on the tally. On the Higgs, I agree that the discovery matters more for our understanding of nature than a clock does. But the Physics Prize is for the original work, and my own round-1 proposal for B001 (Della Negra, Jenni, Virdee) differed from yours and from most others, which shows that the committee does not agree on who the original people are. I am not willing to settle that by choosing three names at the last stage for the sake of weight. If the committee wants to treat B001 seriously, it needs a settled attribution, which I do not think we have. I would therefore not make it a second part, but I would keep it as an alternative.

responses.point: Kroll names overlap with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize as his main reservation, and asks whether the lattice clock stands as a distinct achievement and whether to wait for the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I think the citation can answer your distinctness question, and I have written mine accordingly: it names the invention and realization of the lattice clock and the magic-wavelength trapping, and does not mention frequency combs or accuracy records alone. On waiting, I disagree. The strongest evidence we have is the agreement between independent laboratories, and that already exists; deferring until the SI second is redefined would tie the prize to a metrological decision that is not ours to wait for, and it would not increase our confidence in who invented the lattice clock.

responses.point: Danielsson says that the lattice clock is useful rather than existential and that horizon-scale imaging of black holes (B016) or moire quantum matter (B046) change how we picture the world; his configuration keeps B046 and B016 as alternatives.
responses.response: I understand the pull of those candidates, and B046 was in my own ballot as a full trio. But I ranked it last for reasons that have not changed: the superconducting mechanism remains disputed, the experimental credit among several groups is not settled by the three names given, and the field is young. For B016, I share your suggestion that the polarization and dynamics results should come first. The clock may be less existential, but it is verified and it does not have those open questions, and I do not think a prize should wait for a bigger idea when the verified one is ready.

responses.point: Eriksson says that the missing Cao credit is a real weakness for B046 and that this is one reason B046 is no longer first for them, and that the lattice clock has scientific merit, attribution and maturity lined up better than any other candidate.
responses.response: I agree with this, and I would add that it is the reason I do not think B046 should be added as a second part even for those who rank it highly. A second part must have a defensible credit within the three-person limit, and with Katori and Ye already taking two of the three allowed names, B046 would need an attribution of one person, which it does not have. A single-part prize is the honest result of this shortlist.

uncertainties: Whether Katori's lattice proposal and first strontium clock, and Ye's record accuracy and many-body clock, are best seen as one achievement or as two contributions of unequal originality; I cannot verify the early priority dates for Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and others from the material in front of me.
Whether the committee will accept that the magic-wavelength lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, or will see it as an incremental step on a line already honoured.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second makes this the right year, which I think it does but others disagree.
Whether the omission of the other lattice-clock groups will be judged as unfair, a point on which I have no further evidence to settle the matter.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. I have no conflict for B013 and I know of no connection to Katori or Ye. B015 (aberration-corrected electron optics) is in my own field, electron microscopy, and I know that community through the IFSM, so I would recuse myself from any decision on B015, and I have therefore not advocated it in this round; it appears only as an alternative, and the chair should treat my views on it as those of an interested party. I share an institution (Chalmers) with Göran Johansson, whose B054 is no longer part of his preferred configuration. No other conflict is apparent from my profile.
